title: Scaling our existing tagging system with Hybrid Graph-Semantic Search
summary: How we moved from a manual tagging system to a state-of-the-art hybrid graph-semantic relevance and retrieval platform with knowledge…
body_text: Scaling our existing tagging system with Hybrid Graph-Semantic Search Tripadvisor 15 min read · Oct 27, 2025 -- Press enter or click to view image in full size How we moved from a manual tagging system to a state-of-the-art hybrid graph-semantic relevance and retrieval platform with knowledge graph, and the dramatic effect it had on how we catalog, validate, and surface information for travelers. By Sabreena Rajan , Varuni Gang , Meng Pan and Amir Rad We typically start our blog posts with a sentence or two about how many reviews we store, how many points of interest we represent, or how many travelers trust us to provide relevant accurate data about their favorite travel destinations. Needless to say, it’s a lot of data and if you don’t believe us, just check here , here , or here . What we don’t often talk about however, are the real challenges we constantly face in making sure that travelers are consistently presented with the right information. When you visit Tripadvisor , we want you to immediately see what matters most to you, whether that’s “kid-friendly spots in Rome” or “late-night jazz in London”. Making that happen is harder than it sounds! Behind the scenes, experiences like these are powered by our tagging system, which assigns labels, concepts, or topics to content in our system in the form of a “tag”. For example, when we tag a POI (or point of interest, such as a restaurant or museum) in Rome as kid-friendly , it makes it easy to find for families planning their trip. In short, tagging helps us to both understand our content and to present it back to travelers in meaningful and relevant ways. But tagging at scale comes with hidden challenges. If tags are outdated or incomplete, travelers can’t find what they’re looking for. A restaurant may have switched from vegetarian to vegan, or a trend like “digital nomad” may emerge before our taxonomy can catch up. Those gaps directly impact the traveler experience. Today, most of our tags exist only on POIs and historically they haven’t always been updated automatically as places evolve. At our scale, this makes discovery inconsistent for travelers. Furthermore, we’ve got millions of related pieces of content like images, forum posts, and articles, that all exist in the system but are not tagged at all. These challenges prompted us to build a new, scalable approach to tagging. We are excited to share a new feature that is now live in our Android and iOS apps: interest-based POI shelves . These personalized shelves on the app homepage are used to showcase a collection of restaurants, hotels and attractions that are tailored to each traveler’s interests. In this blog post, we’ll walk through how we built them, why they matter to our users, and how they represent a major paradigm shift in how we tag at Tripadvisor. New feature: Interest-based POI shelves At Tripadvisor, shelves are organized by type of content: hotels, attractions, restaurants. Until recently, they were mostly static, meaning that they were manually created and didn’t automatically update. We’ve now introduced a new set of shelves organized by interests, such as Italian cuisine in New York, Luxury escapes in Paris, or Art & culture in Milan. These shelves are dynamically created for each traveler by identifying their most relevant interests and by fetching the associated POIs through newly created tags. Press enter or click to view image in full size New feature: Interest-based shelves on our application home pages The tags are the important piece of the puzzle here since they make it possible to surface POIs that were previously hidden in interest-based searches. For example, a bar with live music that hadn’t been tagged, or a pasta spot that wasn’t linked to Italian cuisine. Without these tags, travelers searching for those interests would have missed them entirely and we wouldn’t have been able to surface them in any kind of dynamic way. Our internal testing shows that these interest-based shelves have proven highly popular with members, achieving a CTR (click-through rate) over 10% which is significantly higher than other content on our app home page. We also found that CTR was highest for more specific interests, like theme parks. This insight highlighted the importance of stronger taxonomy design and more accurate tagging to capture detailed interests. While the feature itself was a hit, it served a deeper purpose. It pushed us to rethink how we could build and scale our tagging system, in order to improve accuracy, expand coverage, and uncover new relationships between tags. By strengthening this foundation, we could make it possible to connect travelers with the right experiences faster and at a scale that was previously unachievable. Why tags needed a rethink Tripadvisor uses tags to map shared attributes across places. Tags that represent amenities like pool or Wi-Fi, styles like romantic, or cuisines like Indian or Thai. They are critical for enabling travelers to filter properties like hotels and attractions, power shelves and maps, improve site search and boost SEO traffic. To manage these tags at scale, we rely on a Knowledge Graph (KG). Think of a knowledge graph as a map of relationships. Each node is an entity in the real world such as a hotel, a restaurant, a city, or a cuisine type and each edge is a relationship between those entities such as located_in_Paris , offers_Italian_Cuisine , or is_part_of_hotel_brand . When a restaurant has live music, that information is stored as an edge in the graph. Press enter or click to view image in full size A visualization of POI data in our knowledge graph Our graph is incredibly powerful because it allows us to run structured queries at scale. For example, we can ask: “Find all hotels in Rome with rooftop pools”, or “Show family-friendly resorts in Mexico that also have waterparks”. But the results are only as good as the tags and the relationships that power it. If a hotel isn’t tagged, it will not show up in the search results. What’s more, if relationships are incomplete (say a hotel has a “waterpark” tag but is missing the “family friendly” tag) the traveler’s experience could feel patchy. Above, the Charlie’s POI is not tagged with the “Live Music” tag Until recently, tags were: Created and maintained via business rules, often leading to outdated or inconsistent coverage. Rarely updated when places changed, for example if a restaurant went vegan, a traveler couldn’t discover it until the owner or staff updated it. Difficult to govern at scale with overlapping concepts like beach resort, family beach resort and luxury beach hotel Slow at capturing new trends, which often appear in reviews long before a formal tag exists. This made it very difficult for travelers to find them. Clearly, our existing tagging process wasn’t keeping pace with the richness and velocity of traveler data. That’s why refreshing how we tag the content became central to unlocking better discovery. From idea to proof of concept As we built our other recent RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) applications like review summaries and traveler FAQs , we realized that other leading companies and research projects were showing promise with innovations in combining RAG and Knowledge Graphs. These approaches were often referred to as GraphRAG. In parallel, leading graph databases like Neo4j and Neptune began supporting vector indexes for semantic search. This was exciting to us because it demonstrated that knowledge graphs could now do more than answer structured, tag-based queries; they could now also help improve tag coverage and even evolve our existing taxonomy. For example, the graph could answer not only predefined queries, but also dynamic ones like “live music in New York,” powered by semantic search over reviews. To test this, we launched a three-week prototype in Neo4j with a simple goal to: mine unstructured review text with semantic search for queries like “Live music in New York” combine these signals with structured graph traversal to validate or add the right tag-to-property connections determine if these new graph capabilities could scale in practice Because these features were still in the early stages of adoption, we encountered a few obstacles. Documentation and best practices were scarce, vector index–based search in graphs lagged behind standalone vector databases, and features like prefix filtering weren’t yet available. To work around this, we built multiple vector indexes per geo/type combination. Even so, the early results were encouraging. By combining structured traversal for existing tags with vector retrieval over reviews, we managed to identify several relevant and under-tagged POIs. Even better, when a certain topic or query wasn’t yet represented by a tag, we were able to propose it as a new one. Most importantly, we proved that we could develop a scalable approach to dynamically identify tag-to-property connections and new tags, and represent them in the graph for future structured retrieval. We shared these findings with product leaders, showed early examples of how it could improve discovery, and secured investment to productionize the idea. Over the following six months, we scaled the proof of concept into an MVP. We tested how well this approach worked at global scale and measured the impact of improved tag coverage on real travelers. How Hybrid Graph-Semantic Relevance works To properly scale the tagging of our content it was important for the search to optimize for recall, so that we could capture all relevant properties for a given tag. Since reviewers express essential ideas in many ways, we implemented rigorous validation to ensure that each tag assignment properly reflected a tag’s meaning and that the right POIs were captured. For example, one restaurant may only have a jazz performance on weekend evenings, while others host live music every night. We want to capture all restaurants that offer live performances. To achieve this, we developed an extensive multi-step pipeline that applies cutting-edge machine learning techniques and models to ensure accurate and scalable tagging. Preparing and ingesting data Every search and recommendation system starts with data. At Tripadvisor, we have an abundance of it: POIs, Geos, Tags, and reviews. The problem is that they are stored scattered across our data warehouse, and aren’t directly usable. To address this, we built a two-step data preparation and ingestion pipeline to load data into the Knowledge Graph with the data model below. Like any robust pipeline, it supports both full load and incremental loads. Press enter or click to view image in full size A high level representation of our data model Data preparation Our ETL collects data from multiple sources and preprocesses it for recommendations. This includes filtering out inactive POIs and selecting only recent reviews, since outdated ones don’t reflect a POI’s current state. Since we want to enable semantic retrieval, we generate embeddings for tag, destination and POI names using MPNet and review sentence embeddings using GTE (reviews chunked by sentence). Ingestion We ingest data to Neo4j using Spark connectors to ensure parallelized performance. The following challenges required special handling: Avoiding deadlocks Graph databases like Neo4j can lock nodes when adding multiple edges with the same source or target, causing deadlocks in many-to-many relationships. This happens often between Tags and POIs. Instead of implementing a complex backoff system, we adopted a smart hybrid approach by partitioning data by tag, ingesting all tag-POI edges in parallel within each partition, and then processing partitions sequentially. Because tags are roughly 1000 times fewer than POIs, this method avoided race conditions efficiently. Enabling partial search within vector indices Our project required semantic search across a combination of tags, destination, and POI names along with review sentences, however Neo4j currently does not support searching within a subsection of a vector index. A naive solution would have been to create multiple global vector indices for each of the above, and filtering the review sentences post graph retrieval, however that would be costly and nondeterministic. Instead, we created a separate vector index for each destination to hold the review sentence embeddings. The retriever now searches only the index relevant to the destination, making queries efficient and scoped. Press enter or click to view image in full size A “30 thousand foot” view of our ingestion pipeline Graph-Semantic retrieval To retrieve an extensive list of candidate properties, our first step was to introduce two types of searches over knowledge graph: Tag based retriever This retriever searches across all tags in the database which are determined to be most similar to the query (for example, live music or all-inclusive ). The query is mapped into vector space, and tags above a similarity threshold are selected. Associated POIs are then fetched from the graph. Final ranking combines tag-query semantic similarity with the strength of the tag-POI relationship, using the existing relevance score. Semantic search retriever This retriever scans reviews stored in the graph to find those semantically similar to the query, and then retrieves the associated POIs. Each POI is ranked based on both the similarity of its matched reviews to the query and the number of relevant reviews found for it. These retrieval techniques combine to balance precision and coverage. The tag retriever always runs first, returning places with strong tag matches. If the number of tag results is insufficient, the semantic search retriever kicks in to surface additional POIs from review text. For example if the query is “Japanese restaurants that serve sushi”, the tag retriever returns all places tagged as Japanese restaurants, while the semantic search retriever returns those where reviews mention sushi. Together, they deliver a complete set of results, both officially tagged restaurants and those that were validated through customer reviews. These results are de-duplicated and ranked by a combination of popularity and relevance, ensuring the most meaningful POIs rise to the top. Press enter or click to view image in full size A high level view of our retrieval chain Refining relevance with models After retrieval, we re-score each candidate POI using a cross-encoder model. In our evaluation, the Jina reranker (cross-encoder model) consistently outperformed other models at capturing fine-grained context and the interactions between queries and review sentences, though it comes with higher computational cost. We applied thresholds to the reranker’s output relevance scores, ensuring that only POIs with high-confidence match are retained, delivering the precision necessary for reliable tagging. To further refine results, we introduced an LLM-based judge to validate whether each POI truly aligns with the tag’s intended meaning. Finally, we applied a multi-factor scoring method that combines POI relevance with popularity, ensuring highly relevant and widely favored places rise to the top. For example, when tagging Chinese Hotpot restaurants in London, our initial Graph-Semantic Retrieval yields roughly 4000 locations. Over 90% turned out to be Chinese restaurants that don’t serve hotpot. The review below was identified in this stage due to its semantic similarity with our query ‘Chinese Hotpot.’ Although it’s considered by our travellers to be one of the best Chinese restaurants, it does not serve hotpot. Press enter or click to view image in full size A traveler review taken from Tripadvisor.com The re-ranker filtered out most of these irrelevant results, but a few nuanced cases remained. For instance, this review was included because it serves Tofu hot pot which our model did not distinguish from Chinese Hotpot: Press enter or click to view image in full size A traveler review taken from Tripadvisor.com To resolve these nuanced cases, the LLM-based judge validated the remaining candidates, leaving a refined list of authentic Chinese Hotpot restaurants that travelers can confidently discover. Here is the LLM’s assessment of the restaurant discussed above: “The reviews do not mention hotpot specifically, and the restaurant is not known for hotpot, focusing instead on various other Chinese dishes.” As for Haidilao Huǒguō The O2: “Haidilao Hot Pot London O2 is specifically known for its hotpot cuisine, with multiple reviews highlighting the variety of hotpot bases, fresh ingredients, and the overall hotpot dining experience. The reviews consistently mention hotpot-related aspects, confirming its relevance to the query.” Turning search into a tagging engine This hybrid search not only powers our shelves but also continuously improves the tagging system and knowledge graph itself. When a traveler query (for example beach, swimming) maps cleanly to an existing tag, we return the tag along with relevant POIs. Any additional POIs that aren’t yet tagged are added as new tag-to-property connections. If a query doesn’t map cleanly to an existing tag, we can still fetch relevant POIs which are validated by review signals, and then scalably add the query as a new tag in the graph. This approach addresses the tag coverage gaps (like missing venues associated with “live music”) and also improves query performance. Once queries become actual tags in the graph, subsequent lookups can rely on computationally-efficient structured graph traversal instead of intensive semantic retrieval, delivering faster results, lower operational cost, and more predictable performance. A high level view of the tagging engine and how we use it to improve our tagging system and knowledge graph In our latest run, we successfully restored 167,000 missing tag‑to‑property connections across 131 existing tags, strengthening discovery where coverage had long been incomplete. In addition, we introduced 133 new tags and established over 414,000 new tag‑to‑property connections, vastly expanding the breadth and accuracy of our tagging system. To ensure accuracy over time, we re-run hybrid graph search every month to capture the latest reviews, to adjust existing assignments and to propose new ones. This closed-loop process is what enabled the interest-based shelves to scale so broadly. For travelers, this means discovering more relevant content even faster, whether it’s the latest food trend, a hidden music venue, or the perfect boutique hotel. Challenges and learnings As with any approach there are always some limitations, some of which we have yet to solve: Factual tags need safeguards. A number of tags in our system are objective, for example, hotel star rankings are awarded by a governing body, based on a very strict criteria. A hotel would not be pleased if we used this approach and accidentally misrepresented their star rating. Similarly, there will always be certain curated tags. For example, the Traveler’s Choice awards that Tripadvisor gives out on a yearly basis. These tags are human governed and will be excluded from automated assignments. Finally, we’d need to address what we call the cold start problem, or what happens when a brand new restaurant, hotel, or attraction opens for business. New POIs are added every day without reviews and will continue to require manual and partner-provided tag assignments. What’s next We plan to scale the approach to dramatically improve traveler experience across Tripadvisor. Beyond POIs, we host a wide range of unstructured and multimodal content such as forums, Q&As, articles, images, and videos. By tagging this content and connecting it in our knowledge graph, we should be able to dynamically surface it based on each traveler’s interests. Imagine discovering your favorite local sandwich shop in Chicago and, alongside it, seeing expert-written articles about the pulled pork sliders or the homemade milk shakes for the destination you are headed to next. This kind of personalization becomes possible simply by tagging and organizing all the different types of content on our platform. We are exploring ways to improve existing tag assignments, adding precision where needed, and removing existing assignments when the latest reviews give us high confidence that they are no longer valid. We believe that building a clearer, more coherent taxonomy and leveraging machine learning to understand neighborhoods of related tags will be invaluable in surfacing new and complementary interests. For example, if a traveler is browsing for beachwear in Huntington Beach, they might also want surf lessons at a nearby shop. Drawing on research in tag taxonomy and community detection on graphs, we can infer that clustered tag relationships help identify related interests even when they aren’t explicitly tagged. On the technical front, we are continuing to refine each step of our approach. For semantic retrieval, we are exploring incremental/delta processing across months to avoid re-evaluating reviews we’ve already processed. This should make the pipeline faster and more cost-efficient. Conclusion Moving from mostly manual tagging to a hybrid graph-semantic relevance platform represents a true paradigm shift. It brings together two of Tripadvisor’s greatest strengths: our rich base of traveler reviews and our modern graph. With appropriate human-in-the-loop (HiTL) processes, this approach will help to keep tags accurate, discover new concepts and make relevant content easier for travelers to find. The project itself also reflects something we value deeply: smart, ambitious teams taking calculated risks to solve problems that matter to travelers. Our goal is to keep increasing the amount of personalized content we can serve, ultimately providing a more meaningful experience for travelers and trip planners alike. It’s the traveler’s job to share their experiences with the world, but it’s our responsibility to make those insights discoverable. Acknowledgements A project of this scale is never the work of one group alone. While the post highlights the machine learning and graph innovations, it was made possible through close collaboration across Product, Engineering, and Data teams. We’d also like to recognize our external partners at Neo4j, whose support and expertise were invaluable in helping us push boundaries of what graph technology can do at scale. Special thanks to Rahul Todkar, Peter Gaidarev, Gianluca Rossi, Scott Pingeton, and Chris Chalifour for their leadership in helping us prioritize this effort, and to our teammates Sonali Syngal, Chuchen Xiong, Rishabh Maheshwari, Joao Miguel Figueiredo Lopes De Simas, Haley Derrod, Long Yao, Abhishek Gurung and Konstantin Buzdin for their contributions throughout the journey. Together, their efforts turned an ambitious idea into a platform that meaningfully improves how travelers discover the world on Tripadvisor.

title: Formal Named Cloud Security Segment Leader in Latio Market Report
summary: Formal recognized as Cloud Security Segment Leader in the 2025 Latio Market Report.
body_text: The Shift within Cloud Security and Privileged Access Management Cloud Security is undergoing the most significant transformation since the rise of CNAPP. As infrastructure, data, and AI systems converge, the traditional separation between Cloud Security and Privileged Access Management (PAM) is disappearing. What used to be distinct layers – runtime protection, posture management, identity access – are now merging into a single continuum of visibility and enforcement. The 2025 Latio Cloud Security Report captures this moment clearly: organizations no longer want multiple, disjointed tools for cloud visibility, access, and enforcement. Instead, they’re moving toward unified access control and data-flow governance, where the same platform can both monitor and mediate how sensitive workloads are touched – by humans, systems, or AI agents. In this shift, Privileged Access Management has re-emerged as the critical enforcement plane for both cloud and on-prem environments. The report highlights that teams are demanding just-in-time access, session-level auditability, and dynamic policy evaluation – not just for administrators but for every service identity interacting with production data. Formal sits at the intersection of this new security model: a cloud-native PAM designed for the data era. Formal’s Unique Differentiation: A Centralized PAM platform Formal was built around a simple but powerful premise: access control should be as programmable and observable as your infrastructure itself. Unlike traditional PAM tools retrofitted for the cloud, Formal acts as a centralized enforcement layer that unifies human and service access under one protocol-aware platform. The Latio Report recognized Formal’s model as a defining innovation in the category, calling out its ability to “deliver visibility, control, and auditability across both cloud and on-prem environments, without sacrificing developer velocity.” Formal combines: Real-time data-flow visualization – mapping exactly how information moves across services and who is accessing what. Policy-driven workflows – codifying rules for requests, approvals, and access, that are automatically enforced at runtime. Adaptive enforcement – redacting, aliasing, or blocking sensitive data before it leaves a secure boundary. Protocol aware connector – supporting databases, APIs, storage systems, SSH + Kubernetes sessions, and AI endpoints. By embedding directly in the data path, Formal turns access into a measurable control plane, not just a governance checklist. The new frontier of access isn’t human – it’s agentic. AI systems, copilots, and automation agents are increasingly touching sensitive production data, running code, and making decisions that affect security posture. The Latio Report calls this the “agent access problem”. What does this mean for the category? It means that we need to extend PAM’s guardrails from human users to AI agents in real time – which is a problem Formal was purpose built to tackle. Formal’s architecture governs both human and machine identities, treating AI agents as first-class citizens in the access model. That means just-in-time credentials, auditable sessions, and sensitive-data controls all apply equally to your engineers, your workloads, and your LLMs. Formal can even alias or redact data as it flows into an AI model, ensuring that sensitive content (eg. PII, secrets, or regulated fields) never leave the approved boundary. This makes it the first PAM platform purpose-built for the AI era, bridging the gap between infrastructure security and AI governance. What this means for us Being named a leader in the 2025 Latio Cloud Security Report validates what our customers have known all along: that visibility and control belong in one platform. We believe that delivering security outcomes cannot come with any tradeoffs. Formal’s mission is to give security and engineering teams a single enforcement layer for everything that touches sensitive data – human, service, or AI. We understand that the boundaries of cloud security are expanding, but the principle remains the same: trust is earned through context, not static permissions. As the industry redefines what “access” means in the age of automation and AI, Formal will continue to push the boundaries of traditional privileged access management – helping organizations move fast while staying secure. title: JBG SMITH Announces Third Quarter 2025 Results
TotalEnergies cède sa filiale GreenFlex au groupe français Oteis pour créer un acteur de référence dans le conseil et les solutions de développement durable
summary: Paris, le 20 octobre 2025 – TotalEnergies et Oteis, groupe français de conseil et d’ingénierie, ont signé un accord en vertu duquel TotalEnergies cédera sa filiale de conseil et de solutions de développement durable GreenFlex à Oteis. Ce projet de cession s’inscrit pour TotalEnergies dans le cadre de sa stratégie de focaliser ses activités sur […]
body_text: Paris, le 20 octobre 2025 – TotalEnergies et Oteis, groupe français de conseil et d'ingénierie, ont signé un accord en vertu duquel TotalEnergies cédera sa filiale de conseil et de solutions de développement durable Green Flex à Oteis. Ce projet de cession s'ins crit pour TotalEnergies dans le cadre de sa stratégie de focaliser ses activités sur la production et la fourniture d'énergies. Fort de plus de 800 salariés et d'une trentaine d'agences en France et en Europe, Oteis Conseil & Ingénierie exerce dans de multiples domaines : Bâtiment, Eau & Aménagement, Infrastructures & Ouvrages d'Art, Industrie. Oteis a connu ces dernières années une forte croissance grâce à sa ca pacité à intégrer de nouvelles équipes et à développer leurs compétences via des acquisitions similaires à celle de Green Flex. Oteis entend capitaliser sur l'expertise de Green Flex en matière de conseil-environnemental et sociétal, performance énergétique et bas-carbone et financement de la transition pour créer un nouvel acteur de référence qui proposera une offre complète de services et de solutions sur leurs marchés respectifs. Pour les équipes de Green Flex, cette opération permettra de se développer sur de nouveaux marchés tout en continuant d'accompagner les entreprises et les territoi res dans leurs enjeux de développement durable, de décarbonation et d'efficacité énergétique. Dans le cadre de l'accord de cession, TotalEnergies deviendra un client majeur de Green Flex en signant un contrat de production de Certificats d'Economie d'Energie . Ce projet est soumis aux conditions usuelles de réalisation, notamment la conduite du processus de consultation des instances représentatives du personnel et l'obtention des autorisations requises par les autorités de la concurrence. *** Contacts TotalEnergies Relations Médias : +33 1 47 44 46 99 l [email protected] l @TotalEnergiesPR Relations Investisseurs : +33 (0)1 47 44 46 46 l [email protected] TotalEnergies sur les réseaux sociaux X : @TotalEnergies LinkedIn : TotalEnergies Facebook : TotalEnergies Instagram : TotalEnergies

body_text: MONDOVI, Wis., September 30, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Marten Transport, Ltd. (Nasdaq/GS:MRTN) closed on the previously announced agreement to sell assets related to its intermodal business to Hub Group, Inc. (NASDAQ: HUBG), effective September 30, 2025. The transaction was structured as an asset sale of certain intermodal equipment, including over 1,200 refrigerated containers, and contracts to Hub Group, Inc. for $51.8 million in cash. About Marten Transport Marten Transport, with headquarters in Mondovi, Wis., is one of the leading temperature-sensitive truckload carriers in the United States, specializing in transporting and distributing food, beverages and other consumer packaged goods that require a temperature-controlled or insulated environment. The Company offers service in the United States, Mexico and Canada, concentrating on expedited movements for high-volume customers. Marten’s common stock is traded on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol MRTN. title: Knowledge share: Insights from the us-east-1 outage on October 20th
summary: We were affected by the major us-east-1 outage on October 20th that disrupted several core AWS services. Here is how we were impacted, how we responded, and what we're doing to make our system more resilient to full region outages in the future.
body_text: On October 20th, 2025, AWS experienced a major outage in their us-east-1 region that affected several core services, including DynamoDB, EC2, IAM, Console access and many others. This outage had a significant impact on Depot, as we run our primary infrastructure in us-east-1 and utilize several key services, including EC2, DynamoDB, SQS, and Lambda. Before we begin, we want to acknowledge the impact this had on folks who rely on Depot for their builds and GitHub Actions runners. We know many of you were impacted by this outage in ways that were frustrating and disruptive. We sincerely apologize for the disruption this caused. A few elements to understand about Depot's architecture Before diving into the details of the outage and how we responded, it's important to understand a few key elements about Depot's architecture that influenced how we were affected by the AWS outage. Our provisioning system for GitHub Actions runners relies heavily on Dynamo, SQS, and Lambda to manage the lifecycle of EC2 instances that are spun up dynamically to service every job request. We run a set of shadow runners per GitHub org connection and store their state in Dynamo. When a job is requested, we place a message on an SQS queue, which is then processed by a set of Lambda functions that read from the queue, check DynamoDB for the runner's state, and make EC2 API calls to launch new hosts as needed. Once the job is complete, we delete the EC2 instances and update the runner state via our control plane. That instance is then never used again. Container build provisioning works in a similar way but without the need for or dependencies on Dynamo directly, as builds are launched directly via our control plane via the EC2 API. But the process still relies on being able to get a fresh EC2 instance launched to service the build request and then we tear it down when complete. Again, never to be used again. Depot Registry today relies on ECR as the backing store for container image manifests and Tigris behind our global CDN to serve the actual layer blobs. Effectively, today, a registry is tied directly to a container build project. Meaning, that if your project is in us-east-1 , half of your registry API lives in us-east-1 and the other half lives globally behind our CDN backed by Tigris. So we have to be able to call ECR to get manifests for images and thus determine which layer blobs to load from Tigris. How the outages unfolded We have several monitors and alerts set up to notify us when container builds or GitHub Actions jobs fail to launch across our platform. In addition, we have alerts for high queue times, errors in our provisioning system, and other key metrics that help us understand the health of our systems. You can find the status page timeline of the incident here . The timeline below summarizes the key events during the incident. At 12:00 AM PT , we began receiving alerts that container builds and GitHub Actions jobs were failing to acquire hosts from our provisioning system for a large percentage of customers. We began investigating the issue. By 12:05 AM PT, we had determined that the bulk of the errors were coming from our us-east-1 region, with secondary errors also from eu-central-1 for a chunk of IAM-specific errors. At 12:11 AM PT , AWS opened its first incident regarding error rates and latencies in us-east-1 . With that incident, we were able to correlate the issues we were seeing with the larger AWS outage. By 12:45 AM PT , we took stock of our systems and determined that we were unable to connect to any DynamoDB tables in us-east-1 , a core component of our provisioning system. Additionally, our provisioning system was unable to process messages from SQS queues because the event triggers between Lambda and SQS were not firing. Any container build or GitHub Actions job requests that were in flight were failing to acquire hosts because EC2 API calls were returning errors or capacity issues. At 1:00 AM PT , we determined that any GitHub Actions job, container build, Depot Cache request, Depot Registry request for projects in us-east-1 were all failing to process. We effectively had no network connectivity to any core AWS services in us-east-1 , including DynamoDB, SQS, EC2, ECR, and IAM. By 2:20 AM PT , we began to see recovery in us-east-1 as AWS restored connectivity to DynamoDB. We were able to resume launching instances via EC2 to serve some container image builds, but capacity remained limited. GitHub Actions jobs were still failing to launch because SQS to Lambda event triggers were still not functioning, preventing our provisioning system from processing job requests. ECR requests began succeeding with some rate limiting, allowing some Depot Registry requests to succeed again. Without event triggers between SQS and Lambda functioning, our provisioning system could not process any GitHub Actions jobs. We also couldn't fail any of those queued requests to another region, as that is work that GitHub Actions is waiting for a runner to complete. We had to wait for AWS to restore this functionality. At 3:50 AM PT , we started to see some recovery in event triggers between SQS and Lambda, but only a few messages were being released. Our provisioning system began processing the backlog of GitHub Actions jobs that had accumulated during the outage. However, the backlog was significant, and the sheer volume of jobs attempting to launch simultaneously was triggering GitHub rate limits for some customers. By 4:30 AM PT , the backlog of GitHub Actions jobs had started to process, but we were still seeing rate limits from GitHub for some customers due to the high volume of jobs trying to launch simultaneously. We were also continuing to see capacity errors in EC2 as we tried to launch a large number of instances simultaneously to process the backlog and service container image builds. At 4:54 AM PT , we observed full recovery of our API and Dashboard services, with container builds fully recovered for x86 and ARM in the region. GitHub Actions jobs were still being processed at a limited rate due to the backlog, event-trigger throttling between SQS and Lambda, and GitHub rate limits. It was at 6:16 AM PT that we were still observing significant delays in SQS to Lambda event triggers, causing a slow processing of the GitHub Actions job backlog. We reached out to AWS support to understand when we could expect full recovery of SQS event triggers to Lambda. The second outage in us-east-1 became visible to us around 7:00 AM PT , when we started seeing errors again in our provisioning system for both container builds and GitHub Actions jobs. We immediately began investigating the issue and found that, once again, we had lost connectivity to the EC2 API and were receiving capacity errors on every request. During the second outage, we observed connectivity issues with DynamoDB, SQS, and EC2. We began evaluating how we could restore at least some build service while the network was unavailable. We confirmed that we could support launching container image builds in our eu-central-1 region, as that region was still fully functional. At 8:23 AM PT , we advised container build customers who could have their container image builds run in the EU to update their project to the EU Central region to restore container build functionality. At the same time, we worked to restore us-east-1 . We then began evaluating if our backup regions for GitHub Actions in us-west-2 and us-east-2 could be used to restore GitHub Actions job functionality. However, we determined that the backup regions lacked the capacity or quotas to support the volume of us-east-1 workloads. That said, we determined that some queuing was better than no runner at all with infinite queuing. By 9:00 AM PT , we had deployed the necessary changes to our provisioning system to divert GitHub Actions jobs to our backup region in us-east-2 . This allowed us to resume servicing some GitHub Actions jobs, albeit with significant delays due to limited capacity in the backup region. With eu-central-1 available for service container builds and us-east-2 available for some GitHub Actions jobs, we were able to restore some functionality for our customers while we worked to restore us-east-1 . We were still seeing significant delays and networking issues across us-east-1 that were impacting our main API, but work was still able to process. At 11:00 AM PT , we began to see EC2 launches succeed again in us-east-1 , but capacity was still minimal. Some container image builds were able to start launching again, but GitHub Actions jobs stuck in that region were still unable to launch, as SQS to Lambda event triggers were down again. By 11:22 AM PT , we saw additional recovery in the region, with more EC2 launches succeeding, but capacity remained very limited. We also started seeing our provisioning system's SQS queues come back online, and our Lambda events began processing. We started seeing some GitHub Actions jobs stuck in the queue start processing again, albeit with heavy delays and not at our normal rate. At 12:05 PM PT , we saw more messages being processed from our SQS queues as AWS increased the rate of event-trigger processing again. But we were still seeing API errors in the control plane, and our ability to launch EC2 instances remained very limited due to capacity constraints in the region. We were mainly down to AWS reducing EC2 throttling and increasing SQS to Lambda event trigger rates for us to have our full capacity restored in the region. By 1:45 PM PT , we started to see SQS to Lambda event triggers returning to normal rates, but had to wait for the full backlog of events to be replayed. EC2 capacity was also starting to recover as AWS continued to reduce the throttling on our account. At this time, any new GitHub Actions jobs were automatically being diverted to us-east-2 to avoid further delays, while container builds were being serviced in eu-central-1 if customers changed their project region. Capacity remained limited in us-east-2 , and AWS was unable to approve our quota increase while the outage in us-east-1 was ongoing. By 3:00 PM PT , we observed full recovery of queue processing for the backlog of GitHub Actions jobs and container builds being launched in us-east-1 , and we were finally processing at full EC2 capacity. We decided to route GitHub Actions jobs back to us-east-1 as the backlog was clearing and capacity was restored. At 3:30 PM PT , we were seeing signs of complete recovery with both container builds and GitHub Actions jobs processing at normal rates again. We began the process of closing the incident. We left our incident open for several more hours throughout the rest of the day to monitor for any additional issues, but none were observed. We worked with high-throughput customers to ensure they were fully caught up on any backlogs of GitHub Actions jobs that had built up during the outage period. This required us to carefully throttle job launches to avoid GitHub rate limits while we worked through the backlog. What we learned and what we're doing about it Incidents like this are always a learning opportunity. Throughout the incident and in our post-incident review, we identified several areas where we can improve our systems and processes to make us more resilient to similar outages in the future. Maintain a warm backup region for GitHub Actions: We realized that our backup regions for GitHub Actions did not have sufficient capacity or quotas to handle the volume of workloads from us-east-1 . This made it incredibly hard for us to fail over to it to service demand anywhere near that of our primary region. We are working on turning us-east-2 into a warm backup region with sufficient capacity and quotas to handle failover in the event of a significant outage. We have completed that work as of today October 28th, 2025. Better container build region failover: We could have restored container build functionality faster if we had rerouted container builds to our eu-central-1 region automatically when we detected the outage in us-east-1 . We have explicitly avoided doing this automatically as several customers have compliance requirements that do not allow their data to be processed in the EU. However, we are exploring options to make this failover process smoother and faster for customers who can have their container builds run in other regions. Removing dependencies on ECR: Depot Registry was impacted during the outage because of its dependency on ECR in us-east-1 . We are exploring options to remove this dependency to make Depot Registry more resilient to regional outages. Conclusion This incident was a big reminder of how vital core AWS services are to Depot. At the rate we launch EC2 instances per second, even a minor service hiccup can have an outsized impact on our ability to serve our customers. This outage shined a light on where we can improve core parts of our system to be more resilient to region outages and also where we can have tighter processes to fail over to backup regions when needed. We are constantly working to improve Depot and make it more reliable. We are committed to being transparent with our customers about the issues we face and how we are working to fix them. We believe in learning from our mistakes to make improvements so that we don't make the same mistake again. If you're not already, we recommend subscribing to our status page to get real-time updates on incidents and maintenance. Kyle Galbraith CEO & Co-founder of Depot Platform Engineer who despises slow builds turned founder. Expat living in 🇫🇷

title: Stop Drowning in Busywork: How AI and MCP Are Revolutionizing Business Automation
body_text: Is your team drowning in repetitive busywork like updating CRMs and managing a flood of emails, pulling them away from strategic goals? The powerful combination of AI agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the solution, automating these workflows to free up your team for high-impact work. This guide explores how this technology can revolutionize your business operations by seamlessly connecting AI to your essential applications. The Problem with "Busywork" Before we dive into the solution, let's acknowledge the problem. A significant portion of the workday is consumed by manual, repetitive tasks. A Workfront survey found that knowledge workers spend only about 39% of their workday on their primary job duties. The rest is spent on administrative tasks, emails, and meetings. This "busywork" not only kills productivity but also leads to employee burnout. Enter AI agents and MCP. Think of AI agents as your digital workforce, capable of understanding and executing complex tasks. MCP, on the other hand, is the universal translator that allows these agents to securely and efficiently interact with the various software platforms your business relies on every day. It's the key that unlocks true, cross-platform automation. Let's explore some real-world examples of how this dynamic duo is transforming key business functions. Supercharging Your Sales with CRM Automation Your Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system, like Salesforce, is the lifeblood of your sales organization. It's a treasure trove of customer data, but keeping it accurate and up-to-date can be a Herculean task for your sales team. The Challenge: Sales representatives often spend a large portion of their time on non-selling activities. According to Salesforce's own "State of Sales" report , reps spend only 28% of their week actually selling. The rest is dedicated to tasks like data entry, scheduling, and report generation. The AI + MCP Solution: An AI agent connected to your Salesforce CRM via MCP can automate a wide range of these tasks. Task Before AI + MCP (Manual) After AI + MCP (Automated) New Lead Entry Manually create new contact and opportunity records. Instantly creates and assigns new leads from web forms or emails. Activity Logging Sales reps manually log calls, emails, and meetings. Automatically logs all communications with a contact. Sales Forecasting Reps spend hours compiling data for weekly forecasts. Generates accurate, real-time sales forecasts on demand. Follow-up Reminders Reps rely on memory or manual calendar entries. Schedules intelligent follow-up tasks based on customer interaction. The Impact: By automating these administrative burdens, you empower your sales team to focus on what they were hired to do: build relationships and close deals. As noted in a Harvard Business Review article , companies using AI in sales can increase their leads by more than 50% and reduce call time by 60-70%. Example of summary of Salesforce activities and sent to Slack Taming the Communication Overload Email and instant messaging are essential communication tools, but they can also be major productivity drains. It's not uncommon for an office worker to receive over 120 emails per day. An AI agent integrated with platforms like Gmail and Slack can help you and your team stay on top of your communications without getting overwhelmed. The Challenge: Knowledge workers can spend over 10 hours per week just in meetings and nearly 6 hours managing emails. This constant context-switching can disrupt focus and hinder deep work. The AI + MCP Solution: Email Triage and Summarization: The AI agent can scan your inbox, identify high-priority emails based on sender and content, and provide you with a concise summary. Automated Responses: For common inquiries, such as requests for information or support tickets, the AI agent can be trained to provide instant, accurate responses. Seamless Slack Integration: The agent can monitor your Slack channels for important keywords or mentions and alert you to conversations that require your attention. It can also be used to automate routine announcements and daily stand-up reports. The Impact: Imagine reclaiming even a fraction of that time. By automating email and communication workflows, businesses can significantly reduce response times and improve overall efficiency. This allows teams to focus on more strategic and collaborative work, a concept explored in Cal Newport's book "A World Without Email." Example of summary of Emails and sent to Slack Boosting Business Intelligence with Google Sheets Automation Spreadsheets are a cornerstone of modern business operations, essential for everything from financial tracking to project management. However, their reliance on manual data entry can create significant bottlenecks. Studies have shown that up to 88% of all spreadsheets contain errors, which can lead to flawed analysis and costly mistakes. The Challenge: Manually entering, cleaning, and consolidating data from multiple sources is not only tedious but also highly susceptible to human error. This can result in inconsistent data, delayed reporting, and a significant drain on employee time, preventing teams from focusing on more strategic, high-value work. The AI + MCP Solution: Automated Data Entry and Consolidation: An AI agent can connect to various data sources—like CRM systems, marketing platforms, or other spreadsheets—and automatically pull information into a master Google Sheet in real-time. This eliminates the need for manual copy-pasting and ensures data is always current. Intelligent Data Analysis and Summarization: AI can analyze the data within your sheets to identify trends, generate summaries, and even perform sentiment analysis on customer feedback. For instance, it can automatically categorize expenses or highlight sales figures that are outside the norm, providing actionable insights without manual effort. Dynamic Report and Alert Generation: The agent can be configured to automatically generate and distribute reports on a recurring schedule. It can also monitor key metrics and send real-time alerts via email or messaging apps when specific thresholds are met, such as when inventory levels drop below a certain point or a project milestone is reached. The Impact: Automating your Google Sheets workflows drastically reduces the risk of human error and frees up valuable employee time for more strategic initiatives. By transforming static spreadsheets into dynamic, intelligent systems, businesses can ensure data accuracy, accelerate decision-making, and gain a more reliable, up-to-the-minute view of their operations. Example of dumping sales data to Google Sheets The Klavis AI Advantage At Klavis AI, we solve the biggest problem holding back AI assistants: tool overload . When an AI has too many options to choose from, it gets confused and fails. Our flagship product, Strata , fixes this with a simple yet powerful idea. Instead of showing the AI all your tools at once, Strata reveals them step-by-step, only showing what’s relevant for the immediate task. Think of it as giving the AI a simple menu instead of a 1,000-page instruction manual. This approach delivers clear benefits: Boosts AI Accuracy: By focusing the AI, we see a huge jump in performance. Strata is over 15% more successful at completing tasks in popular apps compared to standard methods. Unlocks True Scale: Most systems break when trying to manage a few dozen tools. Strata is built to handle thousands of tools across all your business applications, enabling far more powerful automation. Simple and Secure: We handle the tricky security and user authentication behind the scenes, making it incredibly easy and safe for developers to connect their apps. Quick Start Guide Login to Klavis AI , with production ready 50+ applications available in hand. Follow the OAuth instruction and authorize Klavis AI to access the applications. Then one click to add the MCP to your favourite MCP client or AI agent. It's that easy! For more information, check out the documentation . Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. Is it difficult to set up AI and MCP for my business? Not at all. Platforms like Klavis AI are designed to make the integration process as simple as possible. With pre-built connectors for a wide range of applications and a user-friendly interface, you can get started with AI-powered automation without needing a team of developers. 2. Is this technology secure? Security is a top priority. MCP is designed with enterprise-grade security features, including OAuth 2.0 support for secure user authentication and multi-tenancy authentication for enterprise deployments. This ensures that your data is always protected. 3. How is this different from tools like Zapier? That's an excellent question. Tools like Zapier are fantastic for creating simple, trigger-based automations (" if this happens in App A, then do that in App B"). They work based on pre-defined, linear workflows. The combination of AI agents and MCP represents the next generation of automation. Instead of a rigid, pre-set recipe, you have an intelligent agent that can understand a complex goal and figure out the steps to achieve it. Feature Trigger-Based Automation (e.g., Zapier) AI Agent + MCP Automation Logic "If-This-Then-That" "Understand goal and execute multi-step plan" Example "When a new email arrives with 'invoice', save the attachment to Google Drive." "Find the latest quarterly sales report in my Google Drive, summarize the key findings, and draft an email to the leadership team with the summary." Flexibility Low - follows a strict, pre-defined path. High - can adapt, use multiple tools in sequence, and handle ambiguity. In short, AI + MCP allows for more dynamic, conversational, and complex automation that more closely resembles how a human assistant would work.

title: Cryoport Continues to Set New Benchmarks for the Global Regenerative Medicine Supply Chain
summary: First Global Supply Chain Solutions Company to Achieve ISO 21973 …...
body_text: First Global Supply Chain Solutions Company to Achieve ISO 21973 Certification, Ensuring Highest Transport Safety, Traceability, and Integrity Standards for Cell and Gene Therapies NASHVILLE, Tenn. , Oct. 30, 2025 /PRNewswire/ -- Cryoport, Inc. (NASDAQ: CYRX) ("Cryoport" or "the Company"), a global leader in temperature-controlled supply chain solutions for the life sciences, today announced that Cryoport Systems, a Cryoport company, has successfully achieved certification under ISO 21973:2020, the international standard for transportation of human cells for therapeutic use published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). This milestone underscores Cryoport Systems' commitment to safety and traceability within supply chain management of the rapidly expanding cell and gene therapy industry. First introduced in 2020, Cryoport Systems participated in the Standards Coordinating Body working group that developed the ISO 21973 requirements. The final ISO 21973 standard provides comprehensive guidelines for managing the environmental control, equipment, processes, logistics, and information involved in transporting therapeutic cells, where any deviation could mean the loss of a life-changing or life-saving treatment. Living cells require precise conditions to remain effective. Therefore, monitoring those specific conditions and ensuring the shipping environment has been maintained is crucial for the viability of regenerative medicine therapies and patient outcomes. The ISO 21973 requirements minimize the risks associated with temperature excursions, contamination, and chain of custody breaches. Jerrell Shelton, Chairman & CEO of Cryoport, stated, "With the first and only ISO 21973 certification in the global supply chain solutions market, this achievement further solidifies our position as a pioneer in the life sciences industry. Having helped develop this industry standard with the ISO, we have long adhered to it with our proprietary Chain of Compliance® . Now, we're proud to lead the industry in our successful certification of these rigorous requirements. This comes on the heels of winning the 2025 CPHI Award for Supply Chain Excellence for Cryoport Systems' integrated Supply Chain Platform and is yet another example of Cryoport's leadership in the regenerative medicine industry, providing novel supply chain solutions to better serve patients." While the ISO 21973 standard is specifically tailored to the unique demands of regenerative medicine supply chain, Cryoport Systems applies these same standards across the life sciences spectrum, including its reproductive medicine and animal health markets. For more details on Cryoport Systems' ISO 21973 certification and its impact on the regenerative medicine supply chain, visit www.cryoport.com or download the company's whitepaper on the standard. About Cryoport, Inc. Cryoport, Inc. (Nasdaq: CYRX), is a leading global provider of temperature-controlled supply chain solutions for the Life Sciences, with an emphasis on regenerative medicine. We support biopharmaceutical companies, contract manufacturers (CDMOs), contract research organizations (CROs), developers, researchers, and the Life Sciences, in general, with a comprehensive suite of services and products designed to minimize risk and maximize reliability across the temperature-controlled supply chain. Our integrated supply chain platform includes the Cryoportal® Logistics Management Platform, advanced temperature-controlled packaging, informatics, specialized biologistics, biostorage, bioservices, and cryogenic systems, which, in varying combinations, deliver end-to-end solutions that meet the rigorous demands of the Life Sciences. With innovation, regulatory compliance, and agility at our core, we are " Enabling the Future of Medicine™ ." Headquartered in Nashville, Tennessee, our company maintains a strong global presence with operations across the Americas, EMEA, and APAC. For more information, visit www.cryoportinc.com or follow via LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/company/cryoportinc or @cryoport on X, formerly known as Twitter at www.twitter.com/cryoport for live updates. It is important to note that Cryoport's actual results could differ materially from those in any such forward-looking statements. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially include, but are not limited to, risks and uncertainties associated with the effect of changing economic and geopolitical conditions, supply chain constraints, inflationary pressures, the effects of foreign currency fluctuations, trends in the products markets, variations in Cryoport's cash flow, market acceptance risks, and technical development risks. body_text: – Q3 SaaS Monthly ARPU Expands 19% Year-Over-Year to $365 – Company Exceeds Q3 SaaS EBITDA Guidance – Company Generated Q3 Operating Cash Flow of $22 million DALLAS, October 30, 2025 – Thryv Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:THRY) (“Thryv” or the “Company”), the provider of Thryv®, the leading small business marketing and sales software platform, reported an increase in SaaS revenue of 33% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2025. Third Quarter Financial 2025 Highlights: SaaS revenue was $115.9 million, a 33% increase year-over-year SaaS revenue excluding Keap was $99.1 million, a 14% increase year-over-year Marketing Services revenue was $85.7 million, an 8% decrease year-over-year Consolidated total revenue was $201.6 million, an increase of 12% year-over-year Consolidated net income was $5.7 million, or $0.13 per diluted share; compared to net loss of $96.1 million, or $(2.65) per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2024 Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA was $40.8 million, representing an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.3%. SaaS Adjusted EBITDA was $19.6 million, representing an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 16.9% Total Marketing Services Adjusted EBITDA was $21.2 million, representing an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 24.8% Consolidated Gross Profit was $136.5 million Consolidated Adjusted Gross Profit was $140.3 million SaaS Gross Profit was $82.4 million, representing a Gross Margin of 71.1% SaaS Adjusted Gross Profit1 was $84.6 million, representing an Adjusted Gross Margin of 73.0% 1 Defined as Gross profit adjusted to exclude the impact of depreciation and amortization expense and stock-based compensation expense. We believe Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA Margin, and Adjusted Gross Profit provide investors with the financial measures that closely align with our internal processes. We define Adjusted EBITDA (“Adjusted EBITDA”) as Net income (loss) plus Interest expense, Income tax expense, Depreciation and amortization expense, Restructuring and integration expenses, Stock-based compensation expense, and non-operating expenses, such as Other components of net periodic pension cost and certain unusual and non-recurring charges that might have been incurred. Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered as an alternative to Net income (loss) as a performance measure. We define Adjusted EBITDA Margin as Adjusted EBITDA divided by revenue. We define Adjusted Gross Profit (“Adjusted Gross Profit”) as Gross profit adjusted to exclude the impact of Depreciation and amortization expense and Stock-based compensation expense.
